trial_name: Villanueva — Restrictive vs Liberal Transfusion in Acute Upper GI Bleeding (2013)
citation: Villanueva C, Colomo A, Bosch A, Concepción M, Hernandez-Gea V, Aracil C, Graupera I, Poca M, Alvarez-Urturi C, Gordillo J, Guarner-Argente C, Santaló M, Muñiz E, Guarner C. Transfusion strategies for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(1):11-21.
one_liner: In severe acute UGIB, a restrictive transfusion strategy (Hb <7 g/dL) reduced 45-day mortality and rebleeding compared to a liberal strategy (Hb <9 g/dL).

pico.population: Adults with severe acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis, melaena, or both) managed with urgent endoscopy.
pico.intervention: Restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy: transfuse when Hb <7 g/dL, target 7–9 g/dL.
pico.comparison: Liberal red-cell transfusion strategy: transfuse when Hb <9 g/dL, target 9–11 g/dL.
pico.outcome: Primary: Death from any cause within 45 days. Key secondary: Further bleeding, adverse events, transfusion requirements.

background.existing_knowledge: Red-cell transfusion is common in acute UGIB, but optimal haemoglobin thresholds were uncertain. Extrapolation from critical care 'restrictive' trials was limited because acute GI bleeding populations were excluded.
background.knowledge_gap: There were mechanistic concerns that transfusion might worsen portal pressure and rebleeding in portal-hypertensive haemorrhage, and no dedicated RCT existed.
background.hypothesis: In severe acute UGIB, a restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy (threshold 7 g/dL; target 7–9 g/dL) improves outcomes compared with a liberal strategy (threshold 9 g/dL; target 9–11 g/dL).

methods.design: Randomised, single-centre, pragmatic, open-label trial with concealed allocation, stratified by presence/absence of cirrhosis. Intention-to-treat analysis.
methods.setting: Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Barcelona; enrolled June 2003–December 2009.

inclusion: Adults (>18 years) with haematemesis (or bloody nasogastric aspirate), melaena, or both, confirmed by staff.
exclusion: Low-risk presentation (clinical Rockall score 0 with Hb ≥12 g/dL).

methods.intervention: Restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse packed red cells when Hb <7 g/dL; post-transfusion target 7–9 g/dL; 1 unit at a time with reassessment.
methods.comparison: Liberal transfusion strategy: transfuse when Hb <9 g/dL; post-transfusion target 9–11 g/dL; 1 unit at a time with reassessment. Both arms permitted 'off-protocol' transfusion for anaemia symptoms/signs, massive bleeding, or surgery.
methods.blinding: Open-label (strategy-based transfusion; blinding not feasible). Primary endpoint objective (all-cause mortality).
methods.sample_size_power: 430 patients/group (860 total) required to detect ≥5% absolute mortality difference (assumed 10% mortality in liberal arm) with two-sided α=0.05 and β=0.20 (80% power).
methods.primary_outcome: Death from any cause within 45 days.
methods.follow_up: 45 days (primary endpoint); survival presented to 6 weeks.

headline_bullets: 921 randomised; 32 withdrawn after randomisation; ITT analysis of 444 (restrictive) vs 445 (liberal).
Restrictive strategy significantly reduced 45-day mortality (5% vs 9%; HR 0.55; P=0.02).
Further bleeding was lower with restrictive strategy (10% vs 16%; HR 0.62; P=0.01).
Blood exposure was markedly reduced: mean 1.5 vs 3.7 units; 51% vs 14% received no transfusion.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause within 45 days

outcomes_table.note: Definition required haemodynamic instability or Hb drop ≥2 g/dL within 6 hours
Overall complications lower with restrictive strategy
Major driver of cardiopulmonary harm signal

outcomes_table.outcome: Length of hospital stay (days, mean ± SD)
Blood utilisation (RBC units per patient, mean ± SD)

safety: Fewer adverse events overall with restrictive strategy (40% vs 48%).
Significantly fewer transfusion reactions (3% vs 9%) and TACO (<1% vs 4%).
Fewer cardiac complications (11% vs 16%), including 0 vs 8 myocardial infarctions.

domains.notes: Computer-generated random numbers; sealed, consecutively numbered, opaque envelopes; stratified by cirrhosis; blocks of four.

Open-label strategy could influence co-interventions and thresholds for declaring 'further bleeding' or complications; mitigated by standardised definitions and objective primary endpoint (all-cause mortality).
921 randomised; 32 withdrawn after randomisation; analysed 444 vs 445 by intention-to-treat.
Major protocol violation occurred more often with restrictive strategy (39/444 [9%] vs 15/445 [3%]; P<0.001); nonetheless, deviations were <10% in each group and analyses were intention-to-treat.

Groups were similar at baseline (e.g., mean complete Rockall 5.3 ± 2.0 vs 5.4 ± 1.7; shock at admission 28% vs 31% in supplement); population enriched for higher-risk bleeding (low-risk Rockall 0 with Hb ≥12 excluded).

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity appears moderate-to-strong: allocation concealment and objective primary endpoint support causal inference, with the main limitation being open-label delivery and higher (though still <10%) protocol deviations in the restrictive arm.

domains.notes: Adults with 'severe' UGIB (median-to-high Rockall; 31% cirrhosis; 49% peptic ulcer; 21% oesophageal varices) managed in a specialist bleeding unit with rapid access to endoscopy and (for variceal bleeding) portal pressure measurements in a subset.

Benefits likely depend on timely endoscopic and pharmacological haemostasis (e.g., urgent endoscopy, vasoactive agents, PPI) and availability of rescue interventions; applicability may be attenuated where such pathways are delayed or unavailable. Key exclusions: exsanguinating bleeding requiring immediate transfusion; recent acute coronary syndrome/stroke/TIA/peripheral ischaemia; low-risk presentations; and prior recent transfusion.

external_validity.verdict: Findings are highly generalisable to hospitalised, non-exsanguinating UGIB managed with modern haemostatic pathways; generalisability is limited for massive haemorrhage and patients with very recent major ischaemic events.

strengths: Concealed allocation with stratification for cirrhosis.
Clinically meaningful separation in haemoglobin and transfusion exposure.
Mechanistic portal-pressure substudy consistent with clinical outcomes.
limitations: Post-randomisation withdrawals (32) and more protocol violations in restrictive arm (9% vs 3%).
Exclusions limit applicability to exsanguinating bleeding and very recent high-risk cardiovascular events.
Some secondary outcomes could be influenced by care decisions in an unblinded trial.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted, practice-changing RCT with a strong internal validity for its primary outcome, though open-label design and single-centre setting are minor limitations.
strengths: Concealed allocation and objective primary endpoint (all-cause mortality) minimise bias.
Large effect size with consistent benefits across multiple outcomes and a mechanistic substudy.
weaknesses: Open-label design could influence secondary outcome assessment.
Single-centre execution may limit generalisability of the exact protocol.

sections.authors_conclusion: A restrictive transfusion strategy improved 45-day survival and reduced further bleeding and adverse events compared with a liberal strategy in patients with severe acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial is practice-changing, establishing a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb <7 g/dL) as the standard of care for most patients with severe acute UGIB.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospitalised, non-exsanguinating UGIB patients managed with rapid endoscopy and contemporary haemostatic care, particularly those with cirrhosis Child–Pugh A/B.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: A restrictive strategy is safe for patients with exsanguinating haemorrhage or very recent major ischaemic events, who were excluded from the trial.
implementation_caveats: Guidelines recommend a more liberal threshold (e.g., Hb <8 g/dL) for patients with known cardiovascular disease.
Benefit was not demonstrated in patients with advanced cirrhosis (Child–Pugh C).

controversies.notes: Concerns that open-label management could influence rebleeding/rescue decisions and complication ascertainment were raised in published correspondence, although mortality (primary outcome) is less susceptible to bias.

Exclusion of very recent acute coronary syndrome/stroke/TIA and limited data in high-risk ischaemic subgroups meant the 'one-size-fits-all' Hb <7 threshold remained debated, driving guideline nuance (e.g., higher thresholds in known cardiovascular disease).

Benefit was clear in Child–Pugh A/B cirrhosis but not in Child–Pugh C (HR 1.04; wide CI), raising questions about competing risks and whether transfusion strategy meaningfully alters outcomes in advanced liver failure.

context_related_trials.relation: A subsequent cluster-randomised feasibility trial that demonstrated implementing hospital-level transfusion policies in UGIB is feasible but highlighted practice variability and the need for adequately powered effectiveness trials.

unresolved_questions: Optimal transfusion threshold for patients with acute UGIB and concurrent acute coronary syndrome or other high-risk cardiovascular conditions.
Whether a restrictive strategy is beneficial or harmful in patients with Child–Pugh C cirrhosis.

numbers_to_remember: 51% in restrictive arm received no transfusion
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For severe acute UGIB, transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL (target 7–9) to improve survival and reduce rebleeding, reserving a more liberal trigger for patients with massive haemorrhage or recent major cardiac events.
